title: Redwood migration demo: OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood (parity mapping)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Greenleaf Health through an API and Console migration demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together models to Redwood equivalents. Discussed functional parity (generation, chat, embeddings, function calls), streaming differences, cost/latency tradeoffs, Dedicated vs Hosted, and security needs (SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC/on-prem). Agreed on benchmark pilot, security docs, and dedicated quote.
topics: Parity mapping: GPT/Claude/Together -> Redwood model names and behavior
API differences: streaming, function-calling, stop tokens
Console walkthrough: deployments, model pinning, rollouts
Optimize recommendations: batching, quantization, KV cache
Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, data residency, on-prem option

transcript:
Meeting: Redwood migration demo with Greenleaf Health
Date: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Head of ML, Greenleaf), Tom Reed (Eng Mgr), Sophie Lang (Security)

Summary: Quick demo and deep dive on mapping OpenAI / Anthropic / Together usage to Redwood API and Console. Covered parity for generation/chat/embeddings, function calling differences, streaming behavior, cost/latency tradeoffs, Dedicated vs Hosted, and security/compliance concerns. Ended with clear next steps to run a small benchmark and send security/pricing docs.

00:00 Elena Park: ok everyone thanks for joining, i'm Elena, i'm an AE on the inference team at Redwood. Marcus and i will run through a migration demo — mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood.
00:12 Aisha Patel: great, thanks. we use GPT-4 and Claude mostly in prod, and a handful of models from Together for internal RnD, so parity is our big ask.
00:22 Marcus Li: yeah totally. we'll show how you can map model names, replicate function-calling patterns, and what to expect on streaming and token costs. quick question — are you currently on dedicated infra with any provider or purely hosted?
00:33 Tom Reed: we're hosted with OpenAI today, no dedicated GPUs yet. looking to see if dedicated/reserved makes sense for lower p99 latency.
00:41 Marcus Li: perfect, we'll cover that. Sophie, any compliance must-haves we should know about?
00:45 Sophie Lang: we need SOC2 type II, SSO via SAML/Okta, audit logs, and ability to use our KMS for keys. also data residency for PHI-ish metadata — we might need VPC or on-prem options.
00:58 Elena Park: understood. Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages, and our Dedicated offering can be tied to customer managed KMS. we'll send the SOC2 docs after the call.
01:07 Marcus Li: jumping into the parity mapping: on the left you'll see typical OpenAI model usage — gpt-4 / gpt-3.5-turbo, then Anthropic Claude 2, and Together family. we provide Redwood-compatible model aliases to reduce code change. for example, gpt-4 -> redwood/gpt4-compat, gpt-3.5-turbo -> redwood/gpt35-turbo-compat, claude-2 -> redwood/claude2-compat, together-small -> redwood/together-small-compat (note naming is approximate).
01:29 Aisha Patel: so code changes are minimal? like existing calls to openai.ChatCompletion can point to redwood with small param changes?
01:36 Marcus Li: yes, you can often swap endpoints and keep most params. function-calling is supported, but there are differences in how we stream function call chunks versus OpenAI; we have a shim in the SDK to normalize. sometimes stop token behavior varies — we'll show examples.
01:54 Elena Park: i'll share a parity mapping doc with exact examples and sample curl / python snippets.
01:59 Marcus Li: demo time — api.example: live request to redwood/gpt4-compat with streaming enabled. you'll see the p50/p95 token latency is comparable to your current numbers, and cost per token tends to be more predictable on Redwood because of batching and cache optimizations.
02:18 (demo noise)
02:30 Tom Reed: can you talk about KV cache? we have chat sessions with long context and want to avoid re-encoding the prompt every time.
02:38 Marcus Li: yes — we support prefix/KV caching; it's enabled at the route level in the console. it reduces compute per request if you have repeated prefixes or system prompts. in Dedicated you can get more aggressive caching and inline KV stores which lower effective cost.
02:53 Sophie Lang: if we're storing any user context in cache, is that encrypted at rest?
02:57 Marcus Li: yes, at rest encryption by default, and you can integrate your own KMS for key control. also we keep audit logs for cache accesses.
03:08 Aisha Patel: what's the migration effort for embeddings? we use OpenAI embeddings for semantic search.
03:14 Marcus Li: we have drop-in embedding endpoints. vector dimensions may differ across models, but we provide guidance on re-indexing. often we recommend running a small re-embed job during the pilot. performance and cost comparisons are in the parity doc.
03:33 Elena Park: quick note on tooling: Console has per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, and rollout controls so you can canary a new model alias and auto-fallback to a cheaper variant if quality drops.
03:46 Tom Reed: about rollouts — can we pin a user segment to a version? we have experiments that need consistent model versions per user cohort.
03:52 Marcus Li: yes, pinning by your internal user id is supported. you can split traffic, run A/B, or force rollbacks.
04:01 (short crosstalk)
04:08 Aisha Patel: any gotchas with function-calling? we use the structured function outputs and rely on model-suggested args.
04:15 Marcus Li: function-calling works similarly. small differences: argument ordering and null handling can vary; our SDK normalizes types and there's a compatibility layer for existing openai and anthropic call patterns. sometimes you need to set 'preserve_schema' or tweak streaming chunk sizes.
04:33 Tom Reed: cost vs latency — can you summarize tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted?
04:38 Elena Park: Hosted is easiest to start, pay-as-you-go. Dedicated gives reserved GPUs, predictable p99 latency, and lower unit cost at commit levels. For Greenleaf, where latency and data controls matter, a Dedicated pilot is often recommended.
04:52 Sophie Lang: SLA and uptime? we need 99.9 at minimum.
04:56 Elena Park: our Dedicated SLA can be discussed in the enterprise contract; Hosted has standard SLAs but Dedicated is where we can add stronger guarantees and SRE support.
05:07 Marcus Li: quick console walkthrough — creating a route, assigning model alias, enabling KV cache and batching parameters, setting autoscale policies.
05:20 (demo - console navigation sounds)
05:34 Aisha Patel: in the console can we see token-level cost per operation?
05:36 Elena Park: yes — cost breakdown by system/user/total tokens, and historical charts. you can also export CSV for chargeback.
05:48 Tom Reed: what about model quantization? we have strong throughput needs and willing to accept small quality deltas.
05:53 Marcus Li: we recommend per-workload quantization profiles. Redwood Optimize will suggest INT8 or mixed precision and expected quality delta. Dedicated can expose quantized variants for lower cost.
06:06 Aisha Patel: i'm worried about transcription and hallucination differences — we rely on factuality. how do we measure/regress these?
06:12 Marcus Li: we integrate with your eval suites and have quality monitoring tied to prompt sets; automatic regression alerts when quality metrics slip. We'll help set up baselines in the pilot.
06:26 Elena Park: circling back to security, we'll attach SOC2 docs. Sophie, do you need a vendor security questionnaire or is the whitepaper enough?
06:34 Sophie Lang: both please — the whitepaper first, then the questionnaire. and any network diagrams for VPC/topology.
06:40 Elena Park: noted.
06:42 (pause)
06:49 Marcus Li: moving to specifics — API example, mapping function-calling. (reads code) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/completions -H Authorization... body with model: "redwood/gpt4-compat". we show how stop tokens, max_tokens and function call schema map.
07:10 Aisha Patel: do you expose logprobs? we use them for token-level confidence.
07:15 Marcus Li: yes, logprobs are available on most variants, though certain quantized models may restrict them — we'll flag which variants support logprobs in the parity doc.
07:25 Tom Reed: latency numbers — can you share p50/p95 for the model flavors?
07:29 Marcus Li: for hosted gpt4-compat p50 ~120ms per token in our sample bench, p95 around 400ms depending on sequence length. Dedicated p95 can be lower due to pinned capacity. we'll run a bench with your 1k prompts to get exact numbers.
07:46 Aisha Patel: how do we handle rate limits and quotas? we can't have throttling during business hours for certain routes.
07:52 Elena Park: route-level rate limits and burst policies are configurable; Dedicated can give you reserved throughput. Also we do priority routing for enterprise traffic.
08:04 Sophie Lang: auditing — do you keep user-level request logs? retention policies?
08:09 Marcus Li: we keep request-level audit logs, retention is configurable; you can export to your SIEM and we support customer-managed S3 buckets for log export.
08:22 (demo continues — some audio notes)
08:40 Elena Park: ok so next practical step — Marcus will run a small benchmark on our side with a Hosted + Dedicated configuration using your 1k sample. Marcus will share the results and parity notes.
08:52 Marcus Li: yes and i'll attach the exact curl/python snippets.
08:56 Tom Reed: timeline — if the bench looks good, we'd like to kick off a POC before year end. are you able to do that?
09:03 Elena Park: yes, we can aim for a POC the week of 2026-12-29. we'll need an NDA signed and a short scoping doc.
09:12 Sophie Lang: also share any SOC2 evidence and KMS integration docs ASAP.
09:17 Elena Park: will do.
09:20 (brief overlap)
09:28 Aisha Patel: curious — for Together models we sometimes run RLHF variants; any caveats switching those?
09:34 Marcus Li: generally RLHF behavior maps but you should retune temperature and sampling params; we can help with a short tuning pass during the pilot.
09:44 Tom Reed: are there any pitfalls you commonly see during migration?
09:48 Marcus Li: typical ones are embedding vector dimension mismatches, stop token edge cases, and function-call schema validation. also minor differences in tokenization affecting prompt length. we document workarounds and have automation scripts to detect mismatches.
10:04 Elena Park: ok final recap — action items: pricing & dedicated quote, parity doc + examples, security docs, and benchmark dataset. we'll target sending docs within 48 hours.
10:20 Aisha Patel: sounds good, thanks everyone.
10:24 Tom Reed: thanks — look forward to the bench results.
10:27 Sophie Lang: thanks, bye.
10:30 Elena Park: thanks all, talk soon.

Notes: transcription has typical auto-transcribe artifacts; some product names may be slightly off. References to Redwood Optimize/Optimise appear; will confirm exact product naming in follow-ups. Links shared during the call: parity doc (link to be sent), SOC2 + security whitepaper (link to be sent), pricing spreadsheet (link to be sent).
